title: They are Coming for the Penguins: Artem Ivanovich Kirpichenok is in a Shin Bet Prison in Israel
author: Nika Dubrovsky
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/artem.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/10/they-
are-coming-for-the-penguins-artem-ivanovich-kirpichenok-is-in-a-shin-bet-
prison-in-israel/) ![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/artem.jpg)

My friend Artem Ivanovich Kirpichenok would not hurt a fly. On 2 August 2026,
he arrived in Tel Aviv and – somehow – ended up in prison. What we know is
that he was arrested by the Shin Bet, Israel’s secret police. There has been
no contact with him since. There has been no official reason for his
detention. A historian and writer who is unusually gentle and kind has now
disappeared into the Israeli prison system.

Artem was born and lived in St. Petersburg (Russia), although he lived in
Israel for fifteen years and graduated from the Hebrew University (Jerusalem).
He later took a PhD in History from the Department of Slavic Studies at the
Center for Arab-Eurasian Studies. Working as a journalist, Artem wrote for TRT
Russian (Turkey) and Caliber (Azerbaijan), where he reported on the Israeli
policy toward the Palestinians and on the Israeli war on Gaza. In 2018, Artem
travelled to Iran, where he visited several cities and wrote about them on his
personal blog.

During the past few days, agitated about Artem, I have taken refuge in
literature produced in and about our city of St. Petersburg (when we were born
there, it was Leningrad). In March 1901, Maxim Gorky published _Song of the
Stormy Petrel_ about an event in the city: students in the city protested over
the conscription of their fellow student in Kyiv for a war that no-one wanted;
and so, the Tsar’s Cossacks came to attack these students at Kazan Cathedral.
The song appeared inside a longer satirical piece called _Spring Melodies_ ,
which the authorities banned. _Spring Melodies_ is set in a land of birds,
where Siskin – a small bird who stands in for the youth – sings this song.
Gorky slipped the song out of _Spring Melodies_ and published it in the
journal _Life_. That song was later canonized in the Soviet Union as a great
revolutionary song.

I love the accident of it. The most dangerous text of that era slipped by the
censors because it pretended to be a harmless little bird song. I never spoke
with Artem about this song, but it is impossible to imagine that he would not
have – like myself – memorized it and sung it in our Soviet schools.

There are two main characters in the song: the petrel and the penguin. The
petrel fights the storm, ‘soars with pride’, and as the wind picks up,
perishes, but with its dignity intact. The penguin, on the other hand, ‘hides
his fat body among the crags’, and therefore survives the storm. But the storm
has other ideas. To rewrite Gorky’s song, we must add in verses that show how
the storm now hunts the penguin as well – how there is no escape from the
wrath of the storm. Artem Kirpichenok is a charming and impractical man who
belonged to no political party and no activist group, who never donated money
to any political cause or signed any statement. He published books about
history and wrote mostly ironic posts on his personal Facebook page. He was
not a penguin (he held strong views on a range of topics), but he was not a
petrel either (he did not advertise his views for the wider public).

Impossible not to have a view on Israeli government policy these days, but
Artem’s views are not so different than those held by the mainstream Israeli
newspaper _Haaretz_. In which case, the question is what has Artem done and
why has he been sitting in a Shin Bet prison without _habeas corpus_ for a
week? If Artem had been part of a movement or a public figure, then there
would be press releases demanding his release. But he is a private individual.
So, who will stand for someone like him?

To arrest Artem is to make private individuals afraid and to make them
internalize their penguin-like condition, to shut up, and sit quietly in the
corner. Arresting a bespectacled writer with a narrow audience is both easy
and makes for a perfectly instructive example. Before Artem was arrested, it
seemed to many of us – me included – that there were ‘anomaly zones’ out
there: in those anomaly zones, one could be somewhat safe from arbitrary
arrest. It was felt that as long as you did not cross certain well understood
line, you could write, read, and speak about pretty much anything. Don’t join
a party, don’t donate to certain organizations, don’t say certain things. But
the lines that seemed to exist have now been erased and what you whisper in
your kitchen can now get you into a prison cell.

The everyday curdles into a nightmare. The kitchen and the prison are becoming
the same room. We have become like frogs that do not notice that the water in
which they are swimming has started to come to a boil. We have made
straightforward cannibalism normal.

When Artem was arrested, his old blog opponents said, what did he expect,
going to Israel, when he could have sat quietly in Petersburg and minded his
own business. Sorry. That’s just the attitude of the frog. There are no safe
places left. There are no crags left to hide a penguin. Artem is not the hero-
petrel. He is much more like the penguin. And so, it is now getting clear to
us, that the penguin hunt has begun. Anyone at all can be picked up and tossed
into the darkness.

Gorky did not know much about penguins. Although they look defenseless, they
can stand their ground as a pack and peck their way out of trouble; in water,
penguins are agile and fast, forming ‘rafts’ to beat adversaries and escape.
Artem needs his penguins to act in unison. Please make noise for him.

_Nika Dubrovsky is the director of the David Graeber Institute._
